name: JPMorgan Chase

profile.reading:
The corporate address at 2701 West 160th Avenue in Broomfield, Colorado is recorded here under the operator name JPMorgan Chase, drawn from mapping data rather than from a public disclosure by the company. JPMorgan Chase and Co. is one of the largest financial services firms in the United States, and like most global banks it runs a distributed network of technology and operations campuses well away from its Park Avenue headquarters in New York. Those sites typically combine office space for operations, technology, and customer service staff with on premises data processing infrastructure sized to the campus's needs, but companies in the banking and financial services sector routinely decline to publish floor plans, power capacity, or server counts for any individual site, treating that information as a security and business continuity matter rather than a marketing point.

Broomfield sits along the US 36 technology corridor between Denver and Boulder and has become a magnet for large corporate campuses. The city is home to major facilities for Oracle America, Intermountain Health Care, and BAE Systems, and it serves as headquarters for Crocs, Vail Resorts, and Webroot. A financial company locating back office, technology, or processing operations in this corridor would fit a broader pattern among national employers who have moved support functions out of the highest cost coastal markets while staying within reach of a deep pool of technical talent along the Front Range.

No press release, filing, or page on jpmorganchase.com describing a facility at this Broomfield address was found, and the city's own published material on major local employers does not mention JPMorgan Chase by name. That absence is itself informative. It suggests this location, if active, functions as an internal operations or technology site rather than a public facing branch, event space, or flagship office that the bank would promote. Financial institutions size their internal data halls to the needs of specific business lines, whether trading systems, retail banking platforms, or enterprise IT, and those decisions are almost never disclosed at the building level even when the company is otherwise highly public about its overall technology investment. Readers looking for confirmed capacity, tenancy, or construction details for this specific address will not find them published, and that gap reflects standard practice in the sector rather than any unusual secrecy about this site in particular.

reading:
JPMorgan Chase is a publicly traded bank, listed on the New York Stock Exchange as JPM and filing with the SEC under CIK 0000019617, and it is in this registry as an enterprise that runs computing for itself rather than as anyone's landlord. The registry holds a single facility for it, a building at 2701 West 160th Avenue in Broomfield, Colorado, on the northern edge of the Denver metro. The underlying map data tags that structure as a data centre both by building type and by telecom function and names JPMorgan Chase as the operator, and the stored coordinates sit on that address, so at least the location and the tenant are consistent.

Almost nothing else about the site is publicly established, and it is worth being blunt about that. Broomfield is a combined city and county and publishes planning, zoning and economic development material, but no rezoning case, conditional use permit, site plan approval or development agreement naming this building as a data centre has surfaced, and JPMorgan does not appear on the city's published list of largest employers, which in its 2018 form was topped by CenturyLink with about 2,360 people at the former Level 3 Communications campus and Oracle with about 2,000. There is no Colorado Public Utilities Commission docket for the site, which is unsurprising because a load of this size would not require one, and there is no state siting review of the kind Ohio or Virginia would generate. The bank itself does not break out individual data centre locations or specifications in its annual report or its SEC filings, and it has issued no press release about a Broomfield facility.

A figure of roughly 20 megawatts circulates for this building in commercial trackers. It should be treated as unverified. None of those listings attributes the number to a filing, a permit or a company statement, and none says whether it is meant to describe critical IT load, the utility service into the building, installed standby generation or something else entirely. Those are four different quantities and the difference between them is often a factor of two or more. This registry records no critical IT capacity for the site because no source has stated one.

What can be said with confidence is why a bank of this size operates its own halls at all. JPMorgan Chase states that it invests over 18 billion dollars a year in technology, serves 86 million customers and moves about 12 trillion dollars in payments a day. Banking supervisors treat the systems behind those numbers as critical infrastructure, with expectations on operational resilience, recovery time, data residency and the ability to demonstrate control of the environment that are far easier to satisfy in space the bank controls than in shared facilities. Core ledger, payments and settlement workloads are also the least suited to public cloud because they are latency sensitive, heavily regulated and expensive to re architect. That is why the largest banks have kept captive sites even while moving customer facing workloads outward, and it is why an unremarkable suburban office park building can be a genuinely important piece of national payment infrastructure without anyone advertising it.

Denver is a rational place for one. It is seismically quiet, well away from hurricane and coastal flood exposure, cheap to cool for much of the year and far enough from the eastern financial centres to serve as a real recovery site rather than a nearby duplicate.
